note: Concludes both stones reach the ground at the same instant, but the reasoning is garbled and self-contradictory (also says the heavier overtakes the lighter); no valid reason.
Never says weightless; says falling bodies press downward with the same force we feel on our feet when standing, and gravity acts on all alike.
States a simple linear proportion between length and time, a constant ratio.
Says a sensation of buoyancy and being lifted up, then repeats the same questions about buoyancy and balloons and collapses into 'a kind of a kind of'.
Restates loss of weight; says gravity is not a uniform force but varies with distance across the body, and the felt change is a vague relational shift; no acceleration, no clear not-a-force claim.
Feels the floor sink, weight gathering on the feet, violent pressure at knees and ribs; drawn to earth by a force we cannot resist.
Off-topic textbook question list about gas, the barometer and the thermometer; never addresses the elevator.
Says the man does not leave the scale and the scale records the load as weight falling; reads the scale and finds the load.
Says the stone strikes the floor and rebounds like a hammer; concludes force is energy or momentum distinct from weight.
Says the stone lands at the foot of the mast, but the reason is centre-of-gravity talk, not shared forward motion.
Describes cable, pulley and gravity drawing the moon; never says what is felt during the fall.
Restates that the falling man feels no weight; says gravity is a sudden direct thrust acting on all particles at once.
Says the equal-vigour assumption is a fatal error and energy is distributed by the character of the vibration, not frequency alone; no mechanism, nothing about high frequencies.
Philosophical musing about human tendency toward motion; never says where the stone lands.
Talks about weight distributed over a feather, cork and ship; concludes gravity draws every body down equally; never says what is felt.
A sensation of being lifted by an invisible hand with no muscular effort, but also feels air press on his boots; never says weight is gone.
Says gravity is a force drawing all bodies to the earth's centre regardless of substance; weightlessness only as restated from the prompt.
Starts on the line of the Earth's motion, then wanders into star distances and repeats 'at the Pole of the sky' dozens of times.
Feels nothing remarkable, a state of suspension between waking and sleeping; subject to gravity and inertia; never says weight is gone.
Rambles about the iron cable, a 500-pound man and 120,000 dollars; never says what is felt.
Says the fall is a consequence of body balance and the total load carried; ends with the man lying prone; never reaches weightlessness or anything beyond.
Says equal sharing is sound in principle, then that energy is lost in proportion to frequency but limited by the body's capacity; contradictory and no mechanism.
Restates no weight in the fall; says the carriage press is the mass moved, not his own weight; never states what the two cases share, and hedges that weight may return.
Says energy is distributed unequally across the spectrum and confined to particular frequencies; restates the peak, no mechanism.
Says the stone is pulled downward and falls in a curve to strike the ground; the hand is a lever.
Says vibrations cannot all be equal, then that we do not receive all the energy given out, then drifts into a textbook chapter on light as a substance.
Says the medium shapes the ray and moves in concert with its own vibration; ends on glass panes; no explanation of the null result.
Textbook question list, then 'How long will a body fall from a roof fastened to it?' repeated about forty times.
Describes the machine tearing apart; says these are the sensations of the machine, not the person; never says what the person feels.
Says the stone lands ahead of the mast, or does not land on the deck at all.
Says the heavier stone arrives first with greater velocity.
Textbook Q and A, then 'The rate of a pendulum is equal to the amplitude of its vibrations' repeated many times.
Ether and magnet rambling; 'the ether of the ether' and 'the big one is the big one' repeated.
States length proportional to the square of its distance from suspension and wrong numbers (four feet swings twice and a quarter); no square-root rule.
Says the man in the falling cabin feels the weight of his own body during the fall; the carriage man does not fall freely.
Says the scale records displacement into motion, feet of descent, not weight; never says it reads nothing; no acceleration.
Says the falling person and the carriage man both feel pressed back into their seats; then rambles about roof resistance.
Rope-and-ship analogy; gravity draws down and inertia draws up; cut off before stating what the cases share.
Animal spirits explain why we do not notice weight; concludes gravity acts without our assistance.
One line says the stone remains suspended if let go at the right moment, then says it rises and attributes it to the earth's rotation.
Asserts the two speeds are not the same, denying the result.
Rambles that the heavier has greater impetus, then concludes both strike at roughly the same instant because velocity is equalised; no real reason.
Garbled product rule multiplying length by the square of the period and gravity; nonsense numbers; no square-root relation.
Says the scale records the acceleration and a reading proportional to the cable weight; descends with a force greater than gravity.
Pendulum Q and A, then 'What is the diurnal motion of the earth?' repeated.
Question list about a stone in water and wind, repeated; never says where the stone lands.
Attributes the disturbance to some unseen body, perhaps nearer or differently situated; does not place it beyond Uranus.
'What is the weight of the stone / elevator / rope?' repeated dozens of times.
Suspended ball text; 'the thread is not affected by the weight of a ball' repeated.
Says nine feet vibrates at nine feet per second and a longer pendulum has a reduced time of swing.
Says equal sharing is false and energy is given out in varying quantities at unequal frequencies; no mechanism.
Restates the numbers then says the time is in proportion to the length.
Describes watching an elevator fall from outside, stupefied astonishment; never says what weight feels like.
Weighing procedure for the cable at 1,000,000 pounds; 'the cable is found to be of the same weight as the balance' repeated.
'What if the cable breaks, and the elevator...' repeated.
Says velocity is proportionate to mass, so the heavier falls faster; garbled numbers.
Says the stone moves gradually from his hand to the floor, drop by drop.
Question list on dangers of falling, then railway rail counts for every length up to 39,000 yards.
'What is the common notion of the weight of the air?' repeated.
Says the stone strikes forward or astern of the mast, a quarter or half a mile ahead.
A feeling of exhilaration and being free, then mine and rope and pulley questions repeated.
Describes the crash at the bottom and the crushing shock; never says what is felt during the fall.
Starts on knowledge from the sense of weight, then 'the same amount of water was in the same volume in the chamber as in the basin' repeated.
Off-topic textbook section on the radiation of sound with figures; never addresses the stones.
Wrong numbers (nine feet in two seconds, sixteen in one) and says time proportional to the square of the length.
